title: Vector & Semantic Search
summary: Matching by meaning instead of matching by keyword — embeddings, approximate nearest-neighbor search, and where an inverted index stops being enough.

slides.markdown:
Everything so far in this group matches on **words**: an [inverted index](inverted-index) finds documents sharing literal terms with the query. **Semantic search** matches on **meaning** instead — a query for "affordable place to eat" should be able to find a document that says "budget-friendly restaurant" even though they share zero words.

The trick is representing text (or images) as **vectors** — long lists of numbers — positioned so that similar meanings land near each other in that vector space, then searching by distance instead of by shared terms.

slides.sectionTitle: Why keyword search misses "meaning": synonyms, paraphrases, and cross-language matches
slides.markdown:
An inverted index is only as good as the literal terms it stores. It cannot connect "affordable" and "budget-friendly" — different words, same meaning — without extra machinery (a synonym list bolted on top, which needs constant manual maintenance and never fully covers real language). It similarly can't match a paraphrased question against an answer worded completely differently, or match a query in one language against a document in another.

This is the ceiling described back in [Search Fundamentals](search-fundamentals): keyword matching solves "contains these words" well, but "means the same thing" is a fundamentally different problem — one that needs a representation of meaning, not just tokens.

slides.sectionTitle: Embeddings: representing text/images as vectors where distance means semantic similarity
slides.markdown:
An **embedding** is a fixed-length list of numbers (commonly hundreds to a couple thousand dimensions) produced by a trained model, positioned so that semantically similar inputs land close together in that vector space and dissimilar inputs land far apart. "Budget-friendly restaurant" and "affordable place to eat" get mapped to nearby points, even though they share no words, because the model learned meaning from patterns in huge amounts of text.

"Distance" between two vectors is a real, computable number — commonly cosine similarity or Euclidean distance — so "how similar are these two pieces of text" becomes a math operation on two lists of numbers instead of a set intersection on shared terms.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: two differently-worded queries landing near the same document in vector space
slides.markdown:
![Similar-meaning queries and a document clustered in vector space](assets/vector-space-search.svg)

The two differently-worded queries land near each other and near the relevant document, purely because the embedding model captured that they mean similar things — no shared keyword required. The unrelated document sits far away in the same space, which is exactly what "search by distance" is computing.

In practice this space has hundreds of dimensions, not two — the 2D picture is a simplification of the same underlying idea: proximity encodes similarity.

slides.sectionTitle: Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search: HNSW and why exact nearest-neighbor doesn't scale
slides.markdown:
Finding the true nearest vectors to a query means computing the distance from the query to *every* stored vector — fine for a thousand documents, hopeless for a billion, since it's a full scan every single query. **Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN)** search accepts a small chance of missing the exact best match in exchange for sub-linear query time.

**HNSW** (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is the dominant ANN algorithm in production: it builds a multi-layer graph connecting each vector to its nearby neighbors, then searches by starting at a sparse top layer and greedily descending toward denser layers, narrowing in on the right neighborhood without ever comparing against most of the dataset. The trade-off is explicit and tunable — more thorough graph traversal gives higher recall (closer to exact) at the cost of higher query latency.

slides.sectionTitle: Vector databases and vector indexes bolted onto existing stores
slides.markdown:
Two ways teams add vector search in practice. **Dedicated vector databases** (Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, Qdrant) are built from the ground up around ANN indexes, embeddings storage, and metadata filtering as first-class features. **Vector indexes bolted onto existing stores** (pgvector for Postgres, Elasticsearch's/OpenSearch's `dense_vector` field, Redis's vector search) add ANN capability to a database or search engine you likely already run.

The practical trade-off: a dedicated vector database is usually more optimized and feature-rich for pure vector workloads, while bolting vector search onto an existing store avoids running an entirely new system and lets you combine vector similarity with the filtering and relational features you already have. Most teams start with the bolt-on option unless vector search is genuinely the core of the product.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: pure keyword search vs pure vector search vs hybrid
slides.markdown:
| | Keyword (BM25) | Pure vector | Hybrid |
|---|---|---|---|
| Strength | Exact terms, IDs, SKUs, rare proper nouns | Synonyms, paraphrases, cross-language, conceptual matches | Both — gets the strengths of each |
| Weakness | Misses paraphrases, synonyms entirely | Can misfire on exact-match queries (an ID, a product code) | More moving parts to build and tune |
| Needs training data | No | Yes — an embedding model | Yes, for the vector half |
| Typical use | Structured or exact-lookup-heavy search | Conceptual/semantic search products (Q&A, recommendations) | Most production search products today |

**How to decide:** default to hybrid in production — run both a keyword query and a vector query, then merge and re-rank the combined results. Pure vector alone is risky wherever users search by exact identifiers your embedding model was never trained to distinguish precisely.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: shipping vector search with no keyword fallback, so exact-match queries get worse
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Vector search understands meaning, so it should handle every kind of query better than keyword search did."

**Why it's wrong:** embeddings are trained to capture semantic similarity, not exact identity — a query for a specific SKU like "WX-4471-B" or a legal case number has no "meaning" for an embedding model to find nearby matches for, and pure vector search can genuinely return worse results for these than plain keyword matching would have. Teams that replace keyword search outright often regress on precisely the queries their power users relied on most.

**Correct model:** keep keyword search available as a fallback (or, better, run both and merge — a hybrid approach). Reserve pure vector search for the conceptual, fuzzy-meaning queries it's actually good at, and route or blend in exact-match signal for anything that looks like an identifier.
